problem: A point $P$ has Cartesian coordinates $(1,\sqrt{3}).$ What are the polar coordinates of $P?$

examples.knowledge_point: Converting from Cartesian Coordinates to Polar Coordinates: First or Fourth Quadrant
examples.problem: Express the Cartesian point $P (1,-\sqrt{3})$ in polar coordinates.
examples.worked_solution:
The first thing to realize is that the point $P$ lies in the fourth quadrant.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13951963/assets/e346dd6ef21e29cc438747c13907c93b8a2b795f01bd360bed8b9319c514fa24.png)

First, we determine $r\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		r &= \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\[3pt]
		&= \sqrt{1^2 + (-\sqrt{3})^2}\[3pt]
		&=\sqrt{1+3}\[3pt]
		&= 2
	}
$$

We then compute the reference angle $\theta_R\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
		\theta_R &= \left|\arctan\left(\dfrac y x\right)\right|\
		 &= \left|\arctan\left(\dfrac{-\sqrt{3}}{1}\right)\right|\
		 &= \left|\arctan\left(-\sqrt 3\right)\right|\
		 &= \left|-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right|\

		&= \dfrac{\pi}{3}
	}
$$

Since the point lies in the fourth quadrant, we subtract the reference angle from $2\pi,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =2\pi -{\theta }_{R} \\  & =2\pi -\frac{\pi }{3} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar coordinates of $P$ are $\left(2, \dfrac{5\pi}{3}\right).$
